arXiv:2610.08965v1 [math.NT] 06 Oct 2026

More than 83.9% of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are distinct and more than 67.35% are simple and on the critical line

Kristian Muri Knausgård Address: Kristiansand, Norway Email address: kristianmk@ieee.org
Abstract.

Let N⁡(T)N(T) count the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function up to height TT with multiplicity, Nd​(T)N_{d}(T) the distinct ones, and N0s​(T)N_{0}^{s}(T) those that are simple and on the critical line. We prove lim infNd​(T)/N⁡(T)≥1645064/1960733=0.83900​…\liminf N_{d}(T)/N(T)\geq 1645064/1960733=0.83900\ldots; earlier work proves 0.83699​…0.83699\ldots, and a report we have not verified claims 0.83805​…0.83805\ldots. Hence more than 67.80%67.80\% are simple. Also lim infN0s​(T)/N⁡(T)≥0.67353​…\liminf N_{0}^{s}(T)/N(T)\geq 0.67353\ldots; earlier work proves 0.67250​…0.67250\ldots, and reports we have not verified claim 0.6734920.673492. Two estimates of Lamzouri are improved: at least 88.93%88.93\% of the zeros are simple or on the critical line, and the proportions of simple zeros and of zeros on the line average at least 83.67%83.67\%. By the unconditional form of Montgomery’s pair-correlation theorem the energy, a sum of a test function over pairs of zeros, is known asymptotically. A zero of multiplicity dd contributes d2d^{2} to it and nearby zeros contribute too, so a lower bound for such pairs leaves less energy for multiple zeros. The proof has three steps. First, for zeros at least a fixed fraction of the mean spacing apart, a large sieve inequality lets their pairs be used in full, with multiplicities. Second, their contribution is bounded below by a computer-assisted inequality for seven or eight consecutive zeros which distinguishes simple and double zeros. Its correction terms telescope, as increments of a storage function. Third, the test function is chosen to make this contribution large, at the cost of more energy. We also prove upper limits for what such inequalities can give with the two main test functions. The lower bounds and these limits are proved in Lean 4, analytic inputs included. The proofs use three axioms beyond those of Mathlib, one per inequality. Each records that a search program returned true; Lean’s kernel does not check the run itself. This work is an experiment in AI-assisted mathematical research.

Key words and phrases: 
Riemann zeta function, distinct zeros, simple zeros, critical line, pair correlation, computer-assisted proof, formal verification, dissipative systems
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11M26; Secondary 11M06, 11Y35, 68V20, 93D30

1. Introduction

Let N⁡(T)N(T) count the nontrivial zeros ρ=σ+i​γ\rho=\sigma+i\gamma of the Riemann zeta function with 0<γ≤T0<\gamma\leq T, with multiplicity, and let Nd​(T)N_{d}(T) count the distinct ones. The simple zeros conjecture states that every nontrivial zero of the zeta function is simple, so that Nd​(T)=N​(T)N_{d}(T)=N(T) for all TT. It is not known to follow from the Riemann hypothesis, and it is not known to imply it. Under the Riemann hypothesis, Montgomery’s pair correlation conjecture implies that almost all zeros are simple [28]. For 0<γ≤3⋅10120<\gamma\leq 3\cdot 10^{12} the Riemann hypothesis has been verified by counting sign changes on the critical line [32]; the number of sign changes found equals N⁡(T)N(T), which counts with multiplicity, and it follows that these zeros are simple.

Under the Riemann hypothesis more is known: at least 1927\frac{19}{27} of the zeros are simple [5] and at least 0.84770.8477 of them are distinct [6]. The bounds of this paper are unconditional: they do not assume the Riemann hypothesis or any other unproved statement.

Unconditionally, Farmer [13] proved that more than 63.9%63.9\% of the zeros are distinct and Ki and Lee [22, Theorem 5] that more than 70%70\% are; see also Wu [49]. An argument discovered by Claude (Anthropic) [7] and verified by Alpöge and Furman [2], together with a second proof by Lamzouri [25], gave lim infNd​(T)/N⁡(T)≥0.83625​…\liminf N_{d}(T)/N(T)\geq 0.83625\ldots, and Wang [47] improved the constant by about 3⋅10−83\cdot 10^{-8}. Chandru [34] obtained 0.836520.83652 with a computer-assisted inequality for seven points, in a preprint that has not been refereed; the reports [37, 40] state 0.836710.83671 and 0.836720.83672. The first paper in this series [23] proved 0.8369928​…0.8369928\ldots. Santibañez-Leal [36] applied its argument to stronger local inequalities and states 0.83737​…0.83737\ldots. A recent report of D’Souza [12] states 0.83757​…0.83757\ldots, with a formal proof in Lean, and 0.83805​…0.83805\ldots, where one finite inequality is checked outside Lean. We have not verified these reports.

Theorem 1.1.

lim infT→∞Nd​(T)N⁡(T)≥q:=16450641960733=0.83900459675​…\displaystyle\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{d}(T)}{N(T)}\ \geq\ q:=\frac{1645064}{1960733}=0.83900459675\ldots

The gain over [23] is 0.00200.0020, and the larger value of [12] is exceeded by 0.00090.0009.

Corollary 1.2.

Let Ns​(T)N_{s}(T) count the simple nontrivial zeros with 0<γ≤T0<\gamma\leq T. Then

lim infT→∞Ns​(T)N⁡(T)≥ 2​q−1=13293951960733=0.67800919​…\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{s}(T)}{N(T)}\ \geq\ 2q-1=\frac{1329395}{1960733}=0.67800919\ldots
Proof.

A zero that is not simple has multiplicity at least two, so N≥Ns+2​(Nd−Ns)N\geq N_{s}+2(N_{d}-N_{s}), that is, Ns≥2​Nd−NN_{s}\geq 2N_{d}-N. ∎

Corollary 1.2 counts simple zeros anywhere in the critical strip. For this quantity [23] gives 0.673980.67398 in the same way, and [12] states 0.67515​…0.67515\ldots with a formal proof and 0.67610​…0.67610\ldots with the finite inequality just mentioned. The zeros that are simple and on the critical line form a smaller set. Before 2026 the unconditional bounds for zeros on the critical line came from the method of Levinson [27, 8]. The last of them is slightly more than 512\frac{5}{12}, and 0.40750.4075 for zeros that are simple and on the line [33]. For the latter, [2, 25] proved 0.67250​…0.67250\ldots, and [47] added about 7⋅10−87\cdot 10^{-8}. Larger values, obtained along the same lines, are stated in work that has not been refereed: 0.673000.67300 [1], 0.673050.67305 [34], 0.673190.67319 [41], 0.673310.67331 [45, 39], 0.673370.67337 [12], 0.6733990.673399 [11], 0.67340.6734 [51], 0.673410.67341 [3], 0.6734250.673425 [37], 0.6734510.673451 [40], 0.6734760.673476 to 0.6734770.673477 [15, 16, 17, 35] and 0.6734920.673492 [14], the last in a draft pull request to a public git repository; the survey in [12, Section 1.4] names further ones. The values of [51] are stated there as complete formal proofs in Lean. A public list of formal proofs, which admits the three standard axioms of Lean only, has entries up to 0.673480.67348 [9, 26]; they are stated for the number of distinct zeros on the critical line, which is at least N0s​(T)N_{0}^{s}(T), and the proof in [26] obtains the bound for N0s​(T)N_{0}^{s}(T) first. We have not verified these reports, and no result of this paper depends on them: they are cited for comparison and for the origin of ideas. All of the values are smaller than the bound of Theorem 1.3 below, which holds for that number as well. A report [50] claims much larger values, 0.79620.7962 for this quantity and 0.89810.8981 for distinct zeros, from trace moments of order up to six. Its authors grade it as a candidate whose analytic part is not yet verified. In [2, Section 7.2] bounds of this kind, such as 1318\frac{13}{18} from the fourth moment, are derived from a hypothesis on these moments. We do not count this report among the values above. Neither Theorem 1.1 nor Corollary 1.2 says anything about the critical line: a zero off the line is distinct, and it may be simple. For the critical line the method is run with the clipping level c=2c=2 in place of c=6720c=\frac{67}{20} and with a second window, and then it gives the following.

Theorem 1.3.

Let N0s​(T)N_{0}^{s}(T) count the zeros ρ=12+i​γ\rho=\frac{1}{2}+i\gamma with 0<γ≤T0<\gamma\leq T that are simple. Then

lim infT→∞N0s​(T)N⁡(T)≥s0:=16691592478195=0.67353820​…\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{0}^{s}(T)}{N(T)}\ \geq\ s_{0}:=\frac{1669159}{2478195}=0.67353820\ldots

The gain over the bound 0.672500.67250 of [2, 25] is 0.001030.00103, and the gain over the largest of the values above is 4.5⋅10−54.5\cdot 10^{-5}.

Lamzouri [25] bounded two further quantities by the same method. Let N0​(T)N_{0}(T) count the zeros on the critical line with 0<γ≤T0<\gamma\leq T, with multiplicity, and let Ns∪0​(T)N_{s\cup 0}(T) count, with multiplicity, the zeros with 0<γ≤T0<\gamma\leq T that are simple or on the critical line. By [25, Theorem 1.1], the average of the proportion of simple zeros and the proportion of zeros on the line is at least 0.83625​…0.83625\ldots, and the proportion of zeros that are simple or on the line is at least 0.88762​…0.88762\ldots. For the second quantity Chandru [34, (1.10)] states 0.888550.88855, from a seven-point inequality for simple points, in the preprint mentioned above, and [12] states 0.887910.88791. The certificates behind Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 give more for both quantities.

Theorem 1.4.

With s0s_{0} as in Theorem 1.3,

lim infT→∞Ns​(T)+N0​(T)2​N​(T)\displaystyle\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{s}(T)+N_{0}(T)}{2N(T)} ≥1+s02=20736772478195=0.83676910​…,\displaystyle\ \geq\ \frac{1+s_{0}}{2}=\frac{2073677}{2478195}=0.83676910\ldots,
lim infT→∞Ns∪0​(T)N⁡(T)\displaystyle\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{s\cup 0}(T)}{N(T)} ≥33764333797325=0.88916092​…\displaystyle\ \geq\ \frac{3376433}{3797325}=0.88916092\ldots

The first bound comes from the second window and the second bound from the first window, and no further computation is needed (Section 6). The first window was not made for the second quantity. A third window, with a seven-point inequality found for this quantity, gives slightly more.

lim infT→∞Ns∪0​(T)N⁡(T)≥5065215956956375=0.88931500​…\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{s\cup 0}(T)}{N(T)}\ \geq\ \frac{50652159}{56956375}=0.88931500\ldots

In particular the larger of Ns​(T)N_{s}(T) and N0​(T)N_{0}(T) is at least (0.8367+o⁡(1))​N​(T)(0.8367+o(1))N(T), and the zeros that are off the line and not simple have proportion at most 0.11070.1107. The proofs of the four theorems and of the corollary are formalised (Section 8).

The idea

Rescale the zeros so that their mean spacing is one. Fix an even probability density ff on I=[−12,12]I=[-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}], the window, with Fourier transform K⁡(t)=∫f⁡(u)​e−2​π​i​t​u​𝑑uK(t)=\int f(u)e^{-2\pi itu}\,du. A zero on the critical line at rescaled height yy is represented by the wave packet f⁡(u)​e2​π​i​u​y\sqrt{f(u)}\,e^{2\pi iuy}, a unit vector in L2​(I)L^{2}(I), and two such vectors have inner product K⁡(y−y′)K(y-y^{\prime}). Summing the rank-one projections over the zeros on the line, with multiplicity, and adding a Hermitian term for each pair of zeros off the line, gives an operator AA with tr⁡A=N\tr A=N [2, 25]. Two numbers are known about AA. The trace counts the zeros. The energy tr⁡A2\tr A^{2} is given by Montgomery’s pair-correlation theorem in its unconditional form [28, 4]: after a smoothing of ff that is removed at the end,

(1.1) tr⁡A2=(C⁡(f)+o⁡(1))​N,C⁡(f)=∫f2+∬|s−t|​f​(s)​f​(t)​𝑑s​𝑑t.\tr A^{2}=(C(f)+o(1))\,N,\qquad C(f)=\int f^{2}+\iint|s-t|\,f(s)f(t)\,ds\,dt.

The energy is a sum over pairs of zeros. If the zeros on the line are at y1<⋯<yly_{1}<\dots<y_{l} with multiplicities di∈{1,2}d_{i}\in\{1,2\}, their part of it is

(1.2) ∑idi2⏟repeated zeros+∑i≠jdi​dj​K​(yi−yj)2⏟different zeros.\underbrace{\sum_{i}d_{i}^{2}}_{\text{repeated zeros}}\ +\ \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j}d_{i}d_{j}\,K(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2}}_{\text{different zeros}}.

A zero of multiplicity dd contributes dd to the trace and d2d^{2} to the first sum, so repeated zeros cost energy, and the energy is fixed by (1.1). Keeping only the first sum gives tr⁡A2≥3​N−2​Nd\tr A^{2}\geq 3N-2N_{d} and hence lim infNd/N≥(3−C⁡(f))/2\liminf N_{d}/N\geq(3-C(f))/2. With the window that minimises C⁡(f)C(f), due to Montgomery and Taylor [29], this is the bound 0.836250.83625 of [2, 25].

The count behind this is d2≥3​d−2d^{2}\geq 3d-2, with equality for d=1d=1 and d=2d=2: a zero of multiplicity dd counts dd in NN and 11 in NdN_{d}. Zeros off the line and zeros of multiplicity three or more are handled by a lemma of linear algebra (Lemma 2.1), which shows that they cannot bring the energy below this count. The lemma has a price. The zeros that are left enter through tr⁡φc​(G)\tr\varphi_{c}(G) and not through tr⁡G2\tr G^{2}, where GG is their Gram matrix and φc\varphi_{c} replaces the square of an eigenvalue above a level cc by its tangent line. We call this clipping. The second sum in (1.2) is tr⁡G2−∑idi2\tr G^{2}-\sum_{i}d_{i}^{2}, so it can be used in full only where GG has no eigenvalue above cc.

The second sum is the energy of the interaction between different zeros. For a suitable window it cannot be small: there are NN units of multiplicity on a line of length NN, so most zeros have neighbours within a few mean spacings, and a double zero interacts twice as strongly with its neighbours as a simple one. The flat window shows why the window matters: its kernel vanishes at the nonzero integers, and the unit lattice has no interaction at all. Every unit of interaction energy is a unit that is not available for repeated zeros. The idea is to prove a lower bound for the interaction energy that is linear in the number of simple points, the number of double points and the length of the line, and to choose the window so that this bound is large.

The paper [23] proved such a bound of small size. There the second sum entered through a matrix inequality, the main result of that paper [23, Theorem 2]. It bounds the clipped energy from below by a function of the Gram matrix (K⁡(yi−yj))(K(y_{i}-y_{j})) of the points without their multiplicities, and the term so obtained was called the defect. That inequality is not used here, for two reasons. It counts every pair with the weight 11 in place of di​djd_{i}d_{j}, so it cannot reward a double zero more than a simple one. And its lower bound grows only linearly above a second level 1+τ1+\tau, which limits the argument to blocks of about 13001300 points, with a loss in every block. For points that keep a fixed distance from each other neither loss is necessary: the clipped energy is then exactly the second sum in (1.2), with the weights (item (1) below). From [23] we keep the threshold lemma, the operator and the count of the zeros (Lemma 2.1, Section 3). Its local input, an inequality for seven consecutive points without multiplicities imported from work on simple zeros [1, 45, 39, 41], is replaced by one with multiplicities that is proved here. Table 1 puts the two papers side by side, and Figure 1 shows the argument in one picture, for zeros on the line of multiplicity at most two.

What is new

  1. (1)

    Separation removes the clipping. Points closer than θ=1720\theta=\frac{17}{20} are paired off and treated as two-by-two blocks. The remaining points are θ\theta-separated. Remark 3.4 says where the value of θ\theta comes from. For such points the Gram matrix (K⁡(yi−yj))(K(y_{i}-y_{j})) is bounded by a constant, by Selberg’s majorant argument for the large sieve [30, 46]; this is the direct half of an inequality of Ingham type [20, 24]. As a consequence the clipped energy of a separated block is exactly the interaction sum in (1.2), with the weights di​djd_{i}d_{j} (Lemma 2.3, Theorem 2.6). For simple zeros on the critical line this step is due to G. Freund [14]: there the zeros closer than 45\frac{4}{5} are paired off, the Gram matrix of the rest is bounded by a majorant of the same kind, and the seven-point inequality of [17] then gives the value 0.6734920.673492 quoted above without the loss of the block argument of [1]. Disjoint pairs of close zeros were used before in [38]. D’Souza [12] uses the step for points with multiplicities, with a majorant of Beurling–Selberg type. The value of [14] is stated in a draft pull request to a public git repository and not in a preprint; we learned of it from the survey in [12, Section 1.4] when the proofs of this paper were complete, and had found the step independently.

  2. (2)

    A local inequality with a storage function. For seven consecutive separated points with labels di∈{1,2}d_{i}\in\{1,2\} we prove, with computer assistance, an inequality between their spread, their weighted squared overlaps and a reward which is larger for double points (Proposition 3.3). The weights depend on the pair of labels. The inequality also contains functions of the gaps which sum to zero over the six positions; when the inequality is added over all sets of seven consecutive points these terms telescope (Lemma 2.5). For points without labels the lemma with such a correction is in [34, Section 3.3], and a seven-point certificate with a nonzero correction, the increment of a function of five gaps, is in [41]; certificates with a function of the state of a frame, and the bound for the loss by its oscillation, are also in [45]. Local inequalities over all patterns of multiplicities one and two were found independently by D’Souza [12, Definition 5.1]. Our corrections are sums of functions of one gap, which depend on the labels and are bounded. For Theorem 1.3 the inequality is for eight consecutive points without labels (Proposition 5.3); frames of nine points are used in [36, 39, 45] and frames of eight in [26].

  3. (3)

    A window for the interaction. For Theorem 1.1 we take f⁡(u)=1+∑j=16aj​cos⁡(2​π​j​u)f(u)=1+\sum_{j=1}^{6}a_{j}\cos(2\pi ju), which we call the first window; the second window, for Theorem 1.3, and the third window, for Theorem 1.5, have the same form with other coefficients, the second with ten terms. For the first window the plain bound (3−C⁡(f))/2=0.83364​…(3-C(f))/2=0.83364\ldots is smaller than that of the Montgomery–Taylor window, but the interaction is worth about 0.00540.0054 instead of about 0.00080.0008. Windows with further cosine terms, chosen with the local inequality in view, are used for simple zeros in [3, 17, 26, 45].

Two of these devices have names elsewhere. The correction terms of the seven-point inequality are the increments of a storage function in the sense of Willems [48]: the inequality is a dissipation inequality, and summing it along the line leaves only a boundary term (Remark 2.7). And the search for the best certificate is dual to an average-cost optimal-control problem, whose value periodic trial configurations bound from the other side (Remark 7.4). In [41] the correction is called a Bellman coboundary, and [45] speaks of transfer-operator certificates.

One formula

Call (x1,x2,b)(x_{1},x_{2},b) a certificate if the interaction energy, in the clipped form defined in Section 3, of every configuration with n1n_{1} simple and n2n_{2} double points is at least x1​n1+x2​n2−b⋅lengthx_{1}n_{1}+x_{2}n_{2}-b\cdot\text{length}, up to bounded and negligible terms. Then (Theorem 3.2)

lim infT→∞Nd​(T)N⁡(T)≥3−C⁡(f)+x2−x1−b2−2​x1+x2.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{d}(T)}{N(T)}\ \geq\ \frac{3-C(f)+x_{2}-x_{1}-b}{2-2x_{1}+x_{2}}.

The bound of [2, 25] is the certificate (0,0,0)(0,0,0). The bound of [34] is the value of this formula at (195000,0,1500)(\frac{19}{5000},0,\frac{1}{500}), where only the simple points interact. The bound of [23] is a certificate with x1=x2x_{1}=x_{2}, because its argument does not distinguish simple from double zeros. Here (x1,x2,b)=(0.054350, 0.069433, 0.037314)(x_{1},x_{2},b)=(0.054350,\,0.069433,\,0.037314).

For zeros that are simple and on the critical line only the simple zeros on the line may interact, and a pair (x,b)(x,b) with interaction energy at least x​n−b⋅lengthx\,n-b\cdot\text{length} for nn simple points gives lim infN0s​(T)/N⁡(T)≥(2−C⁡(f)−b)/(1−x)\liminf N_{0}^{s}(T)/N(T)\geq(2-C(f)-b)/(1-x) (Theorem 5.1). The bound of [2, 25] is the pair (0,0)(0,0), and in Theorem 1.3, (x,b)=(0.008722, 0.004389)(x,b)=(0.008722,\,0.004389).

How far the method goes

For a fixed window the question of the best constant is a ground-state problem for a one-dimensional gas with two kinds of particles, simple points and double points, and pair interaction di​dj​K​(yi−yj)2d_{i}d_{j}K(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2} at prescribed density. Trial states bound from above what any argument of this type can prove. Section 7 has the proofs and Table 2 there the numbers for distinct zeros; the conclusions are these. The bound of Theorem 1.1 is larger than the ceilings for the windows used before, so a new window was necessary for it. For the first window less than 0.00100.0010 remains, so it cannot give 84%84\%, and within our scheme inequalities for seven consecutive points cannot give more than 0.839160.83916. For every window ff with V⁡(f)≤10​B​(f)V(f)\leq 10\,B(f), a regularity condition that holds for the windows of the table and for the second window, the ceiling is 0.840930.84093 (Corollary 7.9), so less than 0.0020.002 is left. This last ceiling rests on a construction of Alpöge and Furman [2], with a law on periodic configurations that we computed and certified ourselves (Section 7.6).

For zeros that are simple and on the critical line, Theorem 1.3 proves 0.6735380.673538 with the second window, inequalities for eight consecutive points cannot give more than 0.673570.67357, and no lower bound for the pair energy of simple points can give more than 0.673830.67383 (Proposition 7.3). Upper bounds of this kind for other windows are in [16, 45]. For every window of the regularity above the limit is 0.681850.68185 (Corollary 7.9), in agreement with [2, Section 7.2]. Figure 2 shows the numbers for both quantities.

Organisation and formal verification

Each bound is proved in four steps, shown in Figure 1: the energy of the window (Proposition 3.1); a local inequality for seven or eight points (Propositions 3.3, 5.3 and 6.3); the bound for the interaction energy of all separated points that follows from it (Theorem 2.6, Proposition 5.2); and the count of the zeros (Theorems 3.2, 5.1 and 6.2). Section 2 contains the inequalities, with all parameters general. Section 3 proves Theorem 1.1: the operator, the passage from a certificate to a bound, and then the constants. Section 4 describes the verification of the seven-point inequality, Section 5 proves Theorem 1.3, Section 6 proves Theorems 1.4 and 1.5, and Section 7 describes the limits of the method. The proofs of Theorems 1.1, 1.3, 1.4 and 1.5 and of Corollary 1.2 are formalised in Lean 4 on top of the library of [7, 2], which derives the analytic inputs from the axioms of Mathlib and has the machinery for a discretised form of (1.1) for a class of windows; Section 8 states what is proved and what is trusted. The Lean developments, the certificate data and the scripts accompany this paper.11 1 https://github.com/kristianmk/839; the same files, except six settings files of code tools, are attached to the arXiv version of this paper. We refer to them as the accompanying files.

2. The inequalities

Throughout this section ff is an even probability density on II, zero outside II, and K=f^K=\hat{f}. Then KK is real and even, K⁡(0)=1K(0)=1 and |K|≤1|K|\leq 1. All other parameters are general; their values are fixed in Section 3.

For real cc let

φc​(t)=t2−(t−c)+2={t2,t≤c,2​c​t−c2,t>c,\varphi_{c}(t)=t^{2}-(t-c)_{+}^{2}=\begin{cases}t^{2},&t\leq c,\\ 2ct-c^{2},&t>c,\end{cases}

a quadratic saturated to linear growth above the level cc. It is convex and C1C^{1}. For Hermitian XX write tr⁡φc​(X)=∑iφc​(λi​(X))\tr\varphi_{c}(X)=\sum_{i}\varphi_{c}(\lambda_{i}(X)), and X⪯YX\preceq Y when Y−XY-X is positive semidefinite.

For Hermitian XX let X±⪰0X_{\pm}\succeq 0 carry its positive and negative eigenvalues, so that X=X+−X−X=X_{+}-X_{-} and X+​X−=0X_{+}X_{-}=0.

Lemma 2.1 ([23, Lemma 4]).

Let P⪰0P\succeq 0, let QQ be Hermitian with at most pp positive eigenvalues, let A=P+QA=P+Q, and let cc be real. Then tr⁡A2≥2​c​tr⁡A−2​c​tr⁡P+tr⁡φc​(P)−c2​p\tr A^{2}\geq 2c\tr A-2c\tr P+\tr\varphi_{c}(P)-c^{2}p.

Proof.

Write Z=Q−Z=Q_{-}, so that A=(P−Z)+Q+A=(P-Z)+Q_{+}. The cross term is 2​tr⁡((P−Z)​Q+)=2​tr⁡(P​Q+)≥02\tr((P-Z)Q_{+})=2\tr(PQ_{+})\geq 0, since Z​Q+=0ZQ_{+}=0. Hence tr⁡A2≥tr⁡(P−Z)2+tr⁡Q+2\tr A^{2}\geq\tr(P-Z)^{2}+\tr Q_{+}^{2}. Also tr⁡Q+2≥2​c​tr⁡Q+−c2​p\tr Q_{+}^{2}\geq 2c\tr Q_{+}-c^{2}p, because x2≥2​c​x−c2x^{2}\geq 2cx-c^{2}. Since φc​(t)=t2−(t−c)+2\varphi_{c}(t)=t^{2}-(t-c)_{+}^{2}, this is tr⁡X+2−2​tr⁡(X​Z)+tr⁡Z2≥0\tr X_{+}^{2}-2\tr(XZ)+\tr Z^{2}\geq 0 with X=P−c​IX=P-cI. Lemma 2.2 (pinching).

Let φ\varphi be convex and let GG be Hermitian. For any partition of the index set into blocks, tr⁡φ⁡(G)≥∑Btr⁡φ⁡(GB​B)\tr\varphi(G)\geq\sum_{B}\tr\varphi(G_{BB}).

Proof.

Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of each block GB​BG_{BB}. Together these form an orthonormal basis (ea)(e_{a}), and ⟨ea,G​ea⟩\langle e_{a},Ge_{a}\rangle runs over the eigenvalues of the blocks. By Jensen’s inequality for the spectral measure of GG at eae_{a}, ⟨ea,φ⁡(G)​ea⟩≥φ⁡(⟨ea,G​ea⟩)\langle e_{a},\varphi(G)e_{a}\rangle\geq\varphi(\langle e_{a},Ge_{a}\rangle). Sum over aa. ∎

Pairs. A pair of points at index distance s≤6s\leq 6 occurs in the frames at the positions (i,i+s)(i,i+s), always with the same labels. Remark 2.7 (the three devices in other terms).

Lemma 2.3 is the large sieve inequality in Selberg’s form. It is the direct half of an inequality of Ingham type [20, 24]: a gap condition on the frequencies yjy_{j} bounds ∫w​|∑jvj​e2​π​i​yj​u|2\int w\,|\sum_{j}v_{j}e^{2\pi iy_{j}u}|^{2} by a multiple of ∑j|vj|2\sum_{j}|v_{j}|^{2}. The inverse half, which gives observability of vibrating systems, needs a window longer than 1/θ1/\theta and is not used here. Secondly, in [23, Lemma 3] the clipped trace was bounded by a dual certificate, tr⁡φc​(G)≥tr⁡(B​G)−14​tr​B2\tr\varphi_{c}(G)\geq\tr(BG)-\frac{1}{4}\tr B^{2} for every B⪯2​c​IB\preceq 2cI. On a separated block this linear matrix inequality is inactive: the optimal multiplier B=2​GB=2G is admissible and the bound is the identity tr⁡φc​(GS​S)=tr⁡GS​S2\tr\varphi_{c}(G_{SS})=\tr G_{SS}^{2} used above, with nothing lost. The multiplier chosen in [23, Theorem 2] is built from the matrix (K⁡(yi−yj))−I(K(y_{i}-y_{j}))-I without the labels, cut off at the level τ\tau; this is where the weights di​djd_{i}d_{j} and the energy above the level 1+τ1+\tau were given up. Thirdly, (2.3) is a dissipation inequality in the sense of Willems [48]. Let the state of a frame be σ=(g0,…,g4,d0,…,d5)\sigma=(g_{0},\dots,g_{4};d_{0},\dots,d_{5}) and let σ′\sigma^{\prime} be the state of the next frame. Then (2.3) says

α⁡(y6−y0)+∑i<jWi​jdi​dj​K​(yj−yi)2⏟cost of the frame≥∑iκi,di⏟reward+Φ⁡(σ′)−Φ⁡(σ),\underbrace{\alpha\,(y_{6}-y_{0})+\sum_{i<j}W^{d_{i}d_{j}}_{ij}K(y_{j}-y_{i})^{2}}_{\text{cost of the frame}}\ \geq\ \underbrace{\sum_{i}\kappa_{i,d_{i}}}_{\text{reward}}\ +\ \Phi(\sigma^{\prime})-\Phi(\sigma),

so Φ\Phi is a storage function for the supply rate “cost minus reward”, and Lemma 2.5 is the summation along the line, which leaves a boundary term. In another language the correction is a coboundary. The certificate used in [23] has Φ=0\Phi=0.

4. The seven-point inequality

Proposition 3.3 is an inequality in six real variables for each of the 272^{7} labellings. Its proof is a finite search. The proof of record is the Lean development of Section 8, in which the search is a function with a soundness theorem; here we describe what it does. The plan of the search, with a table of lower bounds on grid cells, range minima, a cutoff for long frames and bisection of the widest gap, is that of the verifier of [1].

The search starts from the box [13926/H,kmax/H]6[13926/H,k_{\max}/H]^{6}, where 13926/H<θ13926/H<\theta. Two tests are applied.

The first treats all labellings at once. For a pair e=(i,j)e=(i,j) let Eed​d′E^{dd^{\prime}}_{e} be its term Wi​jd​d′​K​(yj−yi)2W^{dd^{\prime}}_{ij}K(y_{j}-y_{i})^{2}, plus Bid​d′​(gi)B^{dd^{\prime}}_{i}(g_{i}) when j=i+1j=i+1. 5. Zeros on the critical line

Why the level changes. In (3.3) a zero on the line of multiplicity j≥2j\geq 2 that is put into the remainder is credited with 2​c​j−c22cj-c^{2}, and a pair of zeros off the line with 4​c−c24c-c^{2}. For a count of the zeros that are simple and on the line, each of these must be at least 22 per unit of multiplicity. For the double zero and for the pair this is 4​c−c2≥44c-c^{2}\geq 4, that is, (c−2)2≤0(c-2)^{2}\leq 0. So c=2c=2. Theorem 1.1 can use a larger level, because zeros off the line are distinct, and for c=6720c=\frac{67}{20} a pair is credited with 2.182.18, a little more than the energy 22 of two simple zeros. The price of the level 22 is that every block that contains a double point and a second point with nonzero overlap has an eigenvalue larger than 22 and is clipped. At the level 22 we therefore let only the simple zeros on the line interact. Their interaction is treated as in Section 2.

Remark 5.4 (why the gain is smaller).

The gain over 2−C⁡(f)2-C(f) is 0.00150.0015, against 0.00540.0054 for distinct zeros. At the level 22 the double zeros do not interact, and the simple zeros have density about 23\frac{2}{3}. They can avoid each other: a configuration in which gaps near 11 and near 22 alternate has all distances close to integers, where KK is small. The window has to make KK at the integers larger, which costs in C⁡(f)C(f), and this is the balance behind the coefficients aj′a^{\prime}_{j}.

6. Two further counts

The two quantities of Theorem 1.4 are bounded by the same inequalities as before. What changes is the count of the zeros that are not in the Gram part, and for the second quantity the level at which their energy is estimated. The preprint [34] also bounds the zeros of multiplicity at most two, by 0.837360.83736 of N⁡(T)N(T) and by 0.939190.93919 of Nd​(T)N_{d}(T); we do not treat these two counts.

For the average the level must be 22: at the level 6720\frac{67}{20} a simple pair off the line is credited with 2.182.18 only, and it counts as much as a double zero on the line, which costs 44. 7. Structure and limits of the method

This section bounds from above what the method can give. Table 2 collects the results for distinct zeros. The two ceilings for the first window are formalised (Proposition 7.2); those for the two earlier windows (Proposition 7.1) and the last line (Corollary 7.9) are certified by ball arithmetic. The ceilings for the critical line are in Proposition 7.3 and Corollary 7.9.

7.1. A ground-state problem

Consider any labelled configuration (Y,D)(Y,D) on the line in place of the zeros, with N=n1+2​n2N=n_{1}+2n_{2} units of multiplicity in an interval of length NN, and let

ℰ⁡(Y,D)=∑i,jdi​dj​K​(yi−yj)2=n1+4​n2+∑i≠jdi​dj​K​(yi−yj)2\mathcal{E}(Y,D)=\sum_{i,j}d_{i}d_{j}K(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2}=n_{1}+4n_{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}d_{i}d_{j}K(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2}

be its energy. The proof uses three facts about the zeros: tr⁡A=N\tr A=N, tr⁡A2≤(C⁡(f)+o⁡(1))​N\tr A^{2}\leq(C(f)+o(1))N, and that the rescaled zeros lie in an interval of length N+o⁡(N)N+o(N). An argument that uses nothing else applies to every such configuration, so it cannot prove more than

Q∗​(f)=lim infN→∞min⁡{n1+n2N:ℰ⁡(Y,D)≤C⁡(f)​N}.Q^{*}(f)=\liminf_{N\to\infty}\ \min\Bigl\{\frac{n_{1}+n_{2}}{N}:\ \mathcal{E}(Y,D)\leq C(f)\,N\Bigr\}.

The minimum is over configurations on the line with labels in {1,2}\{1,2\} only, and with the energy constraint without the o⁡(1)o(1). Both restrictions make the minimum larger, so Q∗​(f)Q^{*}(f) is an upper bound for what can be proved, not necessarily the exact limit. A certificate (x1,x2,b)(x_{1},x_{2},b) in the sense of Section 3 is a linear lower bound for the pair energy: letting ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 for a fixed configuration and using φc​(t)≤t2\varphi_{c}(t)\leq t^{2}, it gives ℰ≥(1+x1)​n1+(4+x2)​n2−b​spread⁡(Y)−O⁡(1)\mathcal{E}\geq(1+x_{1})n_{1}+(4+x_{2})n_{2}-b\,\spn(Y)-O(1), and with n1=2​(n1+n2)−Nn_{1}=2(n_{1}+n_{2})-N, n2=N−(n1+n2)n_{2}=N-(n_{1}+n_{2}) this is ℰ≥(3+x2−x1−b)​N−(2−2​x1+x2)​(n1+n2)−O⁡(1)\mathcal{E}\geq(3+x_{2}-x_{1}-b)N-(2-2x_{1}+x_{2})(n_{1}+n_{2})-O(1). So for μ>0\mu>0 the constant of Theorem 3.2 satisfies (3−C+x2−x1−b)/(2−2​x1+x2)≤Q∗​(f)(3-C+x_{2}-x_{1}-b)/(2-2x_{1}+x_{2})\leq Q^{*}(f); in particular q≤Q∗​(f)q\leq Q^{*}(f) for the first window. Conversely, since mixtures of configurations make the set of attainable densities convex, one expects from convex duality that the best certificate attains Q∗​(f)Q^{*}(f); we do not need this and do not prove it. Either way the problem is that of the least energy, as a function of the densities of simple and double points, of a one-dimensional system with pair interaction di​dj​K​(yi−yj)2d_{i}d_{j}K(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2}.

7.2. Trial states

Upper bounds for Q∗​(f)Q^{*}(f) come from periodic configurations and their mixtures, in which long stretches of different periodic states follow each other. The energy of a periodic state is a finite sum: K2K^{2} is the Fourier transform of R=f∗fR=f*f, which is supported in [−1,1][-1,1], so for period PP and points yiy_{i} in a period, by Poisson summation,

∑i,i′∑n∈ℤdi​di′​K​(yi−yi′+n​P)2=1P​∑|j|≤PR⁡(jP)​|∑idi​e2​π​i​j​yi/P|2.\sum_{i,i^{\prime}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}d_{i}d_{i^{\prime}}K(y_{i}-y_{i^{\prime}}+nP)^{2}=\frac{1}{P}\sum_{|j|\leq P}R\Bigl(\frac{j}{P}\Bigr)\Bigl|\sum_{i}d_{i}e^{2\pi ijy_{i}/P}\Bigr|^{2}.

The simplest trial states explain the numbers. Let elate_{\mathrm{lat}} be the pair energy per point of the unit lattice of simple points. For the first window K⁡(n)=a|n|/2K(n)=a_{|n|}/2 for 1≤|n|≤61\leq|n|\leq 6 and K⁡(n)=0K(n)=0 for |n|≥7|n|\geq 7, so elat=12​∑aj2=0.02054e_{\mathrm{lat}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum a_{j}^{2}=0.02054. Now take four consecutive lattice sites and replace the four simple points by a simple point, a double point, a simple point and an empty site, with the positions relaxed. This saves pair energy, an amount Δ\Delta per cell, and costs 22 in the diagonal term. A mixture of the lattice and of such cells with a proportion ρ2\rho_{2} of double points has energy 1+elat+(2−Δ)​ρ21+e_{\mathrm{lat}}+(2-\Delta)\rho_{2} per unit of multiplicity, and the constraint ℰ≤C​N\mathcal{E}\leq CN allows

ρ2=C−1−elat2−Δ,soQ∗​(f)≤1−C−1−elat2−Δ.\rho_{2}=\frac{C-1-e_{\mathrm{lat}}}{2-\Delta},\qquad\text{so}\qquad Q^{*}(f)\leq 1-\frac{C-1-e_{\mathrm{lat}}}{2-\Delta}.

For Δ=elat=0\Delta=e_{\mathrm{lat}}=0 this is (3−C)/2(3-C)/2. A window is good when its lattice energy is large and merging saves little.

Table 3 gives the numbers for three windows.

The first window gives up 0.0050.005 in CC and gains 0.0140.014 in the lattice energy (Figure 3).

The entries of the table are enclosed by ball arithmetic, as in Proposition 7.1 below. Better trial states exist for the first window. A mixture of three states of period seven gives 0.8399800.839980: six simple points and one empty site; five simple points and one double point; and the pattern simple, simple, double, empty, double, double, empty. They were found by local optimisation over arrangements of simple points, double points and empty sites on a few lattice sites, with the positions relaxed. We do not claim that they are optimal, and for the two earlier windows we use only the cell of the table.

Proposition 7.1.

For the first window, Q∗​(f)<0.83998Q^{*}(f)<0.83998. For the window of [23], Q∗<0.83843Q^{*}<0.83843, and for the Montgomery–Taylor window, Q∗<0.83823Q^{*}<0.83823. The last two are smaller than the constant qq of Theorem 1.1.

Proof.

For each window we give two or three periodic states with rational positions, all gaps at least 0.990.99, and rational weights wk≥0w_{k}\geq 0. Their energies are evaluated by the formula above in ball arithmetic, and C⁡(f)C(f) by rigorous numerical integration, with the library FLINT/Arb [21]; the data and the script are in the accompanying files. With PkP_{k}, NkN_{k}, lkl_{k} and EkE_{k} the period, the multiplicity, the number of points and the energy of a period, the weights satisfy ∑kwk​Pk≤∑kwk​Nk\sum_{k}w_{k}P_{k}\leq\sum_{k}w_{k}N_{k} and ∑kwk​Ek<C⁡(f)​∑kwk​Nk\sum_{k}w_{k}E_{k}<C(f)\sum_{k}w_{k}N_{k}. So for large MM the configuration is admissible in the definition of Q∗Q^{*}, and its proportion of distinct points tends to ∑kwk​lk/∑kwk​Nk\sum_{k}w_{k}l_{k}/\sum_{k}w_{k}N_{k}. ∎

For the flat window f=1f=1 the kernel K⁡(t)=sinc⁡tK(t)=\sinc t vanishes at the nonzero integers, so the unit lattice of simple points and the lattice of double points with spacing two have no pair energy, and their mixtures give Q∗=56Q^{*}=\frac{5}{6}: for that window nothing can be added to the plain bound (3−C)/2(3-C)/2. For the first window Q∗​(f)Q^{*}(f) lies between qq and 0.839980.83998; with the first window the method cannot give 84%84\%.

7.3. Ceilings for certificates

An inequality for seven consecutive points sees only pairs at index distance at most six. The next statement bounds every lower bound for the pair energy that is linear in n1n_{1}, n2n_{2} and the spread, whatever its proof. Its hypothesis for all pairs holds for every certificate in the sense of Section 3, as was shown in Section 7.1, and its hypothesis with s=6s=6 holds for the certificate of this paper, by Lemma 2.5 with ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

Let ff be the first window. Let x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} and b≥0b\geq 0 be real numbers with 2−2​x1+x2>02-2x_{1}+x_{2}>0 such that, for some constant C3C_{3} and all θ\theta-separated labelled configurations,

that is, 3−C⁡(f)+x2−x1−b≤q¯​(2−2​x1+x2)3-C(f)+x_{2}-x_{1}-b\leq\bar{q}\,(2-2x_{1}+x_{2}). The weights in the accompanying files give q¯=0.8391518​…\bar{q}=0.8391518\ldots. For Theorem 1.3 the same two questions have the same kind of answer. Only simple points interact, and a pair (x,b)(x,b) enters the bound (2−C⁡(f)−b)/(1−x)(2-C(f)-b)/(1-x) through a lower bound for their pair energy. By φ2​(t)≤t2\varphi_{2}(t)\leq t^{2}, a certificate (x,b)(x,b) for the critical line gives, for a fixed set and ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, ∑i≠jK​(yi−yj)2≥x​n−b​spread⁡(Y)−C2\sum_{i\neq j}K(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2}\geq x\,n-b\,\spn(Y)-C_{2}, which is the hypothesis of the next proposition for all pairs. A pair obtained from local data through Proposition 5.2 satisfies the hypothesis with s=7s=7, by (5.4) with ϵ=0\epsilon=0. Unlike Q∗​(f)Q^{*}(f), which bounds every argument that uses only the trace, the energy and the length, the proposition is a statement about the scheme of Section 5 only: its trial states place simple points and give the rest of the multiplicity the energy 22 per unit, with no interaction.

Remark 7.4 (the best certificate as an optimal-control problem).

In the terms of Remark 2.7, finding the best triple for frames of seven points is dual to an average-cost problem for a chain with interactions of range six: a triple can be admissible only if the least mean value of energy−x1​n1−x2​n2+b⋅length\text{energy}-x_{1}n_{1}-x_{2}n_{2}+b\cdot\text{length} per point is nonnegative, and in the corresponding Bellman equation the storage function Φ\Phi plays the role of the relative value function. Periodic trial states are admissible trajectories and bound the value from the other side. We have not proved that certificates of the form (2.3) attain the value of this problem.

7.5. What limits the window

Three requirements compete. The energy constant C⁡(f)C(f) should be small; its minimum 1.32751.3275 is attained by the Montgomery–Taylor window [29]. The lattice energy should be large, which needs Fourier coefficients aja_{j} of some size, and these increase CC through the term 12​∑aj2\frac{1}{2}\sum a_{j}^{2} in (3.6). Finally the edge value f⁡(12)f(\frac{1}{2}) must be small enough for the majorant. By Remark 3.4 one needs Λ<c2≤1+12​2−2​x1=1.6876\Lambda<\frac{c}{2}\leq 1+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-2x_{1}}=1.6876. For a majorant of the form used in Section 3, f⁡(12)≤g⁡(12)=γ0​(1+sinc⁡θ)2f(\frac{1}{2})\leq g(\frac{1}{2})=\gamma_{0}(1+\sinc\theta)^{2} forces Λ≥2​f​(12)/(θ⁡(1+sinc⁡θ))=1.6700\Lambda\geq 2f(\frac{1}{2})/(\theta(1+\sinc\theta))=1.6700 for the first window. So here it is the edge value of ff that decides whether the separated blocks escape the clipping.

7.6. All windows

The bounds above are for one window at a time. A bound for all windows follows from a construction of Alpöge and Furman [2, Section 7.2]. A window enters the method only through the pair correlation of the zeros tested against R=f∗fR=f*f, which is supported in [−1,1][-1,1]. In [2] a probability law on periodic configurations is used to show that pair correlation in this band cannot give more than about 0.6820.682 for simple zeros. The same construction bounds the quantities of this paper. It has two parts, an inequality and a law. The law of [2] is not public, so we computed a law of the same kind ourselves; it is given with the accompanying files, its properties are certified, and its share of simple points is slightly smaller than the one reported in [2].

Definition 7.5.

Let N≥2N\geq 2 be an integer and τ≥0\tau\geq 0. A law of period NN with error τ\tau is a finitely supported probability law, with rational weights w𝔠w_{\mathfrak{c}}, on NN-periodic configurations 𝔠\mathfrak{c} of distinct points ξi\xi_{i} with labels di∈{1,2}d_{i}\in\{1,2\} and total multiplicity NN per period, such that the form factor

S⁡(j)=1N​∑𝔠w𝔠​|∑idi​e2​π​i​j​ξi/N|2,S(j)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathfrak{c}}w_{\mathfrak{c}}\Bigl|\sum_{i}d_{i}e^{2\pi ij\xi_{i}/N}\Bigr|^{2},

in which the inner sum is over the points of one period, satisfies |N​S​(j)−j|≤τ|N\,S(j)-j|\leq\tau for 0<j<N0<j<N. Its share of simple points is p=1N​∑𝔠w𝔠​n1​(𝔠)p=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathfrak{c}}w_{\mathfrak{c}}\,n_{1}(\mathfrak{c}), where n1​(𝔠)n_{1}(\mathfrak{c}) is the number of simple points of 𝔠\mathfrak{c} in a period.

The condition on S⁡(j)S(j) says that the law has the pair correlation of the zeros in the band [28].

Lemma 7.6 ([2, Section 7.2], [7]).

Let N≥1N\geq 1, τ≥0\tau\geq 0 and let s1,…,sNs_{1},\dots,s_{N} be real numbers with |N2​sj−j|≤τ|N^{2}s_{j}-j|\leq\tau for 0<j<N0<j<N. Let rr be twice continuously differentiable on [0,1][0,1] with r⁡(1)=0r(1)=0. Then

|∑j=1Nsj​r​(jN)−∫01r⁡(u)​u​𝑑u|≤(16​N2+τ2​N)​(|r′​(1)|+∫01|r′′|).\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{N}s_{j}\,r\Bigl(\frac{j}{N}\Bigr)-\int_{0}^{1}r(u)\,u\,du\Bigr|\ \leq\ \Bigl(\frac{1}{6N^{2}}+\frac{\tau}{2N}\Bigr)\Bigl(|r^{\prime}(1)|+\int_{0}^{1}|r^{\prime\prime}|\Bigr).

It follows from two summations by parts; in the Lean library [7] it is the combination of ceiling_stability and abs_Efun_le_of_nearCUE (directory PairCeiling), applied to a continuously differentiable extension of rr from [0,1][0,1]: hypotheses and conclusion involve rr on [0,1][0,1] only.

Suppose that there is a law of period NN with error τ\tau and share of simple points pp, and put τ0=16​N2+τ2​N\tau_{0}=\frac{1}{6N^{2}}+\frac{\tau}{2N}. Let ff be an even probability density on II, twice continuously differentiable on II, let R=f∗fR=f*f,

and δ0=2​τ0​V​(f)/(B⁡(f)+2​τ0​V​(f))\delta_{0}=2\tau_{0}V(f)/(B(f)+2\tau_{0}V(f)).

    Suppose that all gaps in the configurations of the law are at least gg, and let 0<θ≤min⁡(g,1)0<\theta\leq\min(g,1). Part (b) is the statement for the scheme of Section 5: its hypothesis is that of Proposition 7.3 for all pairs, now for any window and any separation up to min⁡(g,1)\min(g,1).

Proof.

(a) A configuration with labels in {1,2}\{1,2\} and NN units of multiplicity per period, of which n1n_{1} are simple points, has (N+n1)/2(N+n_{1})/2 points per period. So the law has on average 1+p2\frac{1+p}{2} points per unit of multiplicity. By the Poisson formula, the energy per period of a configuration 𝔠\mathfrak{c} of the law is E𝔠=N​R​(0)+2​∑j=1N−1R⁡(j/N)​S𝔠​(j)E_{\mathfrak{c}}=N\,R(0)+2\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}R(j/N)\,S_{\mathfrak{c}}(j) with S𝔠​(j)=|∑idi​e2​π​i​j​ξi/N|2/NS_{\mathfrak{c}}(j)=|\sum_{i}d_{i}e^{2\pi ij\xi_{i}/N}|^{2}/N. by Lemma 7.6 with sj=S⁡(j)/Ns_{j}=S(j)/N and r=Rr=R: on [0,1][0,1] the function RR is twice continuously differentiable up to the endpoints, R⁡(1)=0R(1)=0 and R′​(1)=−f​(12)2R^{\prime}(1)=-f(\frac{1}{2})^{2}. The unit lattice of simple points has energy R⁡(0)=C⁡(f)−B⁡(f)R(0)=C(f)-B(f) per point. A mixture, in the sense of Proposition 7.1, of the lattice with a share δ\delta of the multiplicity and of the configurations of the law with the share 1−δ1-\delta has energy at most C⁡(f)−δ​B​(f)+(1−δ)​2​τ0​V​(f)C(f)-\delta B(f)+(1-\delta)2\tau_{0}V(f) per unit of multiplicity, and δ+(1−δ)​1+p2\delta+(1-\delta)\frac{1+p}{2} points. All periods equal the multiplicities, so the mixture is admissible in the definition of Q∗Q^{*} for every rational δ>δ0\delta>\delta_{0}. The argument of Proposition 7.1 uses only that the weights are rational, that there are finitely many states and that their points are distinct. Let δ\delta tend to δ0\delta_{0}. The last sentence follows from Section 7.1.

(b) Let Y𝔠Y_{\mathfrak{c}} be the set of simple points of a configuration 𝔠\mathfrak{c} of the law. It has period NN and n1​(𝔠)n_{1}(\mathfrak{c}) points per period, and it is θ\theta-separated. Let e𝔠e_{\mathfrak{c}} be its pair energy per period, the sum of K​(y−y′)2K(y-y^{\prime})^{2} over the ordered pairs of distinct points with yy in one period. for the unit lattice, which is θ\theta-separated as well. Multiply the first inequality by (1−δ0)​w𝔠/N(1-\delta_{0})w_{\mathfrak{c}}/N, sum over 𝔠\mathfrak{c}, and add δ0\delta_{0} times the second. With s¯=δ0+(1−δ0)​p\bar{s}=\delta_{0}+(1-\delta_{0})p the left side is s¯​x−b\bar{s}\,x-b. The mean of n1+4​n2n_{1}+4n_{2} per unit of multiplicity is p+2​(1−p)p+2(1-p), so by the bound for the mean energy in (a) the right side is at most

(1−δ0)​(C⁡(f)+2​τ0​V​(f)−2+p)+δ0​(C⁡(f)−B⁡(f)−1)=s¯−(2−C⁡(f)),(1-\delta_{0})\bigl(C(f)+2\tau_{0}V(f)-2+p\bigr)+\delta_{0}\bigl(C(f)-B(f)-1\bigr)=\bar{s}-(2-C(f)),

where the terms (1−δ0)​2​τ0​V​(f)(1-\delta_{0})2\tau_{0}V(f) and δ0​B​(f)\delta_{0}B(f) cancel by the choice of δ0\delta_{0}. Hence 2−C⁡(f)−b≤s¯​(1−x)2-C(f)-b\leq\bar{s}\,(1-x), and s¯=p+(1−p)​δ0\bar{s}=p+(1-p)\,\delta_{0}. ∎

Proposition 7.8 (a law of period 256256).

There is a law of period 256256 with error 10−3010^{-30}, supported on 256256 configurations with rational points, in which all gaps are at least 0.9980.998, and with share of simple points p=0.6818276195​…p=0.6818276195\ldots

Proof.

The law is in the accompanying files: the points have twelve decimals, and the weights have the denominator 106010^{60}. That the labels are 11 or 22, that the multiplicities add up to 256256 in each configuration, the gaps, that the weights are nonnegative with sum 11, and the value of pp are checked in rational arithmetic. Each 256​S​(j)256\,S(j) is a polynomial with rational coefficients in the numbers cos⁡(2​π​j​ξi/256)\cos(2\pi j\xi_{i}/256) and sin⁡(2​π​j​ξi/256)\sin(2\pi j\xi_{i}/256) with rational ξi\xi_{i}. It is enclosed by ball arithmetic with FLINT/Arb [21] at 600600 bits, and the enclosure lies within 10−3010^{-30} of jj. A second program, which shares no code with the first and uses the interval arithmetic of mpmath [43], repeats all checks. ∎

Corollary 7.9.

Let ff be as in Theorem 7.7 with V⁡(f)≤10​B​(f)V(f)\leq 10\,B(f). Then Q∗​(f)<0.84093Q^{*}(f)<0.84093. If 0<θ≤0.9980<\theta\leq 0.998 and (x,b)(x,b) is as in Theorem 7.7(b), then (2−C⁡(f)−b)/(1−x)<0.68185(2-C(f)-b)/(1-x)<0.68185.

Proof.

For the law of Proposition 7.8, τ0=16⋅2562+10−30512<2.5431316⋅10−6\tau_{0}=\frac{1}{6\cdot 256^{2}}+\frac{10^{-30}}{512}<2.5431316\cdot 10^{-6}, and δ0\delta_{0} increases with V⁡(f)/B⁡(f)V(f)/B(f), so δ0≤20​τ0/(1+20​τ0)<5.0861⋅10−5\delta_{0}\leq 20\tau_{0}/(1+20\tau_{0})<5.0861\cdot 10^{-5}. With p<0.6818277p<0.6818277 the two bounds of the theorem are below 0.840930.84093 and 0.681850.68185. ∎

For the four windows of Table 2, V⁡(f)/B⁡(f)V(f)/B(f) is at most 33, 5.25.2, 5.35.3 and 9.09.0, and for the second window it is at most 5.75.7 (ball arithmetic), so the corollary applies to them. We do not know whether laws with triple points give a smaller constant, nor whether some window attains (1+p)/2(1+p)/2.

How the law was found. For a finite set of configurations, the laws with N​S​(j)=jN\,S(j)=j for 0<j<N0<j<N that are supported on this set are the solutions of NN linear equations in nonnegative weights, and pp is linear in the weights. The least pp is therefore the value of a linear programme. A further configuration 𝔠\mathfrak{c} improves the programme if its reduced cost

n1​(𝔠)N−y0−∑j=1N−1yj​|∑idi​e2​π​i​j​ξi/N|2\frac{n_{1}(\mathfrak{c})}{N}-y_{0}-\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}y_{j}\Bigl|\sum_{i}d_{i}e^{2\pi ij\xi_{i}/N}\Bigr|^{2}

is negative, where y0,…,yN−1y_{0},\dots,y_{N-1} are the dual variables of the current solution. To find such a configuration is again a ground-state problem, now for labelled points with the pair interaction −didi′∑jyjcos(2πj(ξi−ξi′)/N)-d_{i}d_{i^{\prime}}\sum_{j}y_{j}\cos(2\pi j(\xi_{i}-\xi_{i^{\prime}})/N). We alternate between the linear programme, solved with HiGHS [19], and a local search for configurations of negative reduced cost; this is column generation [18]. The search starts from perturbations of the configurations in use and from neighbours of them in which two simple points are merged, a double point is split, or a double point is moved. It runs in floating point and is a heuristic. This is harmless, because Theorem 7.7 holds for every law: at the end the points are rounded to rationals, the weights are recomputed for the rounded points from the NN linear equations in high precision and rounded to rationals with sum 11, and the result is certified as in the proof of Proposition 7.8. After the rounding the equations hold up to the error, which is why the definition allows one. Each period starts from configurations of the previous one placed one after the other. For the period 256256 a second stage follows. From each configuration in use it runs a chain of moves that change the labels: a double point is moved, two simple points are merged, or a double point is split. The positions are relaxed after every move, and a move that raises the reduced cost is accepted with the Metropolis probability. In 700700 rounds this lowers pp by about 1.4⋅10−61.4\cdot 10^{-6}. Table 4 gives the laws obtained in this way; each of them is certified, and the last one is the law of Proposition 7.8. The programs, the laws and the logs are in the accompanying files.

Comparison with [2]. In [2, Section 7.2] and in the Lean library [7] a law of period 256256 with labels in {1,2}\{1,2\} is used. The library records its error 3⋅10−403\cdot 10^{-40}, the value p0=0.68182868746​…p_{0}=0.68182868746\ldots of its share of simple points, and interval enclosures of its form factor, computed outside Lean. According to the library the law is the optimal solution of a linear programme over periodic configurations and is available from the authors of [2]; it is not among the public files, and we did not use it. That the points of each configuration are distinct is not stated there. If they are, Theorem 7.7(a) with these values gives Q∗​(f)<0.84093Q^{*}(f)<0.84093 for V⁡(f)≤10​B​(f)V(f)\leq 10\,B(f). Our laws were computed from this description, without their data. After the first stage of the search the share of simple points exceeds p0p_{0} by less than 3.1⋅10−73.1\cdot 10^{-7}. After the second stage it is smaller than p0p_{0} by more than 1.06⋅10−61.06\cdot 10^{-6}, and the error of that law, which the second check bounds as well, is below 10−5010^{-50}. So p0p_{0}, the optimum of the finite programme of [2], is not the least share of simple points of a law of period 256256; we do not know the least share. The bound 0.840930.84093 of Corollary 7.9 does not change, and it does not depend on the law of [2]. Our data and programs are public.

In summary, q≤Q∗​(f)<0.83998q\leq Q^{*}(f)<0.83998 for the first window, and Q∗​(f)<0.84093Q^{*}(f)<0.84093 for every window with V≤10​BV\leq 10B. Less than 0.0020.002 separates Theorem 1.1 from this limit.

8. Verification and nature of this work

The formal statement. The accompanying files contain a Lean 4 [10] development, built with Mathlib [42], that proves

theorem distinct_zeros_839 :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T ≥ T₀,
      (1645064 / 1960733 - ε) * (Ncount 0 T : ℝ) ≤ Ndist 0 T
theorem simple_zeros_678 :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T ≥ T₀,
      (1329395 / 1960733 - ε) * (Ncount 0 T : ℝ) ≤ Nsimple 0 T
theorem simple_critical_zeros_673 :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T ≥ T₀,
      (1669159 / 2478195 - ε) * (Ncount 0 T : ℝ) ≤ N0simple 0 T
theorem average_simple_and_critical_8367 :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T ≥ T₀,
      (2073677 / 2478195 - ε) * (Ncount 0 T : ℝ)
        ≤ ((Nsimple 0 T : ℝ) + (N0mult 0 T : ℝ)) / 2
theorem simple_or_critical_8891 :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T ≥ T₀,
      (3376433 / 3797325 - ε) * (Ncount 0 T : ℝ) ≤ NsimpleOrLine 0 T
theorem simple_or_critical_8893 :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T ≥ T₀,
      (50652159 / 56956375 - ε) * (Ncount 0 T : ℝ)
        ≤ NsimpleOrLine 0 T

The counting functions count zeros of Mathlib’s riemannZeta with real part in (0,1)(0,1) and imaginary part in (0,T](0,T]. Ncount counts them with multiplicity and Ndist without. Nsimple counts those of multiplicity one, and N0simple those of multiplicity one with real part 12\frac{1}{2}. N0mult counts, with multiplicity, those with real part 12\frac{1}{2}, and NsimpleOrLine counts, with multiplicity, those that have multiplicity one or real part 12\frac{1}{2}. The multiplicity is the order of vanishing. The first five are definitions of [7], so the first three statements have the form of the formal theorems there for 56\frac{5}{6}, 0.836250.83625 and 0.672500.67250. Four files import only Mathlib and contain the definitions and the six statements, with the proofs left open by design: Challenge839.lean, Challenge673.lean, ChallengeFurther.lean and Challenge889.lean. The four files with Solution in place of Challenge in their names prove the statements. Table 5 says how each result of this paper is established, and Table 6 where the formal results are in the files.

Compared with the first paper. In [23] the matrix inequalities, the count of the zeros and the arithmetic were formalised, and the rest entered the formal statements as hypotheses: the operator and its reduction to matrices, the energy asymptotic, the smoothing, the passage from seven points to all points, and the seven-point inequality itself, which was imported from [45]. Here each of these steps is proved in Lean, so the formal statements are about the zeros of the zeta function and have no hypotheses. Since qq is larger than the constant of [23], the first statement contains a formal proof of the bound of that paper as well.

What is reused. The development extends the library of [7, 2], which derives from Mathlib the explicit formula, the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula [44] and the Montgomery–Vaughan inequality [31]. It has the machinery for the trace and the second moment of a discretised form of the zero operator for a class of windows, and the resulting statements for the zeta function for two windows. That operator is a finite matrix indexed by a grid of heights; zeros enter through the values of the transform of the window at the grid, and the bandwidth is λ​log⁡T\lambda\log T with λ<1\lambda<1. Two constants in that library were relaxed: the lower bounds 12\frac{1}{2} for two normalised moments of the window became 18\frac{1}{8} and 14\frac{1}{4}. The reason is that our window is not monotone on [0,12][0,\frac{1}{2}] and has to be scaled down to satisfy the variation bounds of the class. The patch changes 1414 files and no headline statement of the library. Mathlib itself is used unchanged, at the revision fixed by the library.

What is new. In order of the proof:

  • •

    the window ff in the class of the library, its moments, and the energy constant Aλ+λ​B\frac{A}{\lambda}+\lambda B with A=∫f2A=\int f^{2}, B=2​∫01u​R​(u)​𝑑uB=2\int_{0}^{1}uR(u)\,du and A+B<C0A+B<C_{0}, so that a bandwidth λ<1\lambda<1 close to 11 gives the energy bound with C0C_{0};

  • •

    the second moment of the zero operator of the zeta function for a general window of the class, which the library had for the flat and the Montgomery–Taylor window;

  • •

    the Gram matrix of zeros on the critical line: for zeros away from the ends of the range its entries are within o⁡(1)o(1) of K⁡(yi−yj)K(y_{i}-y_{j}), and on separated sets it is bounded by c2\frac{c}{2} (Lemma 2.3, with the majorant, its Fourier transform and f≤gf\leq g proved in Lean);

  • •

    Theorem 2.6, with η0=1100\eta_{0}=\frac{1}{100} and C1=152C_{1}=152, and Lemma 2.1 in eigenvalue form;

  • •

    Lemma 2.5 with the checks of the frozen tables;

  • •

    Proposition 3.3, see below;

  • •

    the counting argument of Section 3.

The formal proof follows the written one, with these differences, none of which changes the constant: it works with the discretised operator of [7] at bandwidth λ<1\lambda<1 on the ranges (T,2​T](T,2T] and then sums over dyadic ranges; zeros within T\sqrt{T} of the ends of a range are moved into the indefinite part, together with the zeros of multiplicity at least three and the pairs off the line; the pair blocks are estimated with an explicit loss per point; the Gram bound is stated for a positive semidefinite matrix with the given entries and for distinct points, which is the case in the application; f≤gf\leq g is checked on 4242 dyadic intervals; and β\beta is obtained from thirteen cells of the kernel table and |K′|≤π|K^{\prime}|\leq\pi.

The critical line. Theorem 1.3 has its own development, which repeats this chain for the second window at the level c=2c=2 and reuses every part of the first that does not depend on the window or on the labels. New in it are Proposition 5.2, with η0=1100\eta_{0}=\frac{1}{100} and C1=44C_{1}=44; the inequality (5.4) for frames of eight points, proved in the form with pairs at index distance at most seven; and the count of Section 5. Three points differ from the written proof and do not change the constant. Simple zeros within T\sqrt{T} of the ends of a range go into the remainder, where each costs 44 and carries multiplicity 11; there are o⁡(N)o(N) of them. The Gram entries are known up to a tolerance, so the diagonal entries need not equal 11, and a pair block is estimated by comparison and not by its eigenvalues 1±u1\pm u. And the formal proof uses β=120\beta=\frac{1}{20}, which is all that x≤βx\leq\beta needs. The bound for separated points is used with the constant 1910<2\frac{19}{10}<2, and f≤gf\leq g is checked on 1414 dyadic intervals.

The third window. Theorem 1.5 has a development of the same form, which repeats the chain of the critical line for the third window and ends with the count of part (c) of Theorem 6.2. The three points above apply again, with the cost t2t^{2} in place of 44 for a simple zero near the ends of a range. The formal proof uses β=350\beta=\frac{3}{50} and the constant 1710\frac{17}{10}, and f≤gf\leq g is checked on 2828 dyadic intervals.

The computation. The kernel table of Section 4 is defined in Lean in exact rational arithmetic, and its soundness, the statement that K​(t)2≥vk/228K(t)^{2}\geq v_{k}/2^{28} on each cell, is a theorem. The branch-and-bound search is a Lean function on integers, and its soundness is a theorem: if it returns true on a sound table, Proposition 3.3 holds. What Lean’s kernel does not check is one evaluation, the statement that the search returns true on the table. It is carried out by the tactic native_decide: the table is evaluated by Lean’s interpreter and the search by compiled code, and the outcome is recorded as an axiom. This trusts the Lean compiler, interpreter and runtime for this one computation. The kernel can evaluate the search on single small boxes, as in the third check below, but the whole search is out of reach for it in practice. Certificates of other forms have been checked by the kernel itself: one with 5,6515{,}651 cases in [26], and one through about 1,5001{,}500 generated files in [12]. Three checks support the evaluation. The table computed in Lean, written to a file, agrees with the table of the original certificate in all 209,010209{,}010 entries. A version of the search with counters, built from the same function for a single box, visits 60,467,30960{,}467{,}309 boxes on it and accepts 30,233,65530{,}233{,}655, the numbers of the reference programs in C++ and Python in the accompanying files, which run the same search. And on four small boxes of the domain, among them one around the point of smallest slack, the first test of the search is evaluated by the kernel itself, which proves the inequality there with the standard axioms.

Proposition 5.3 is proved by a second run of the same kind, for boxes of seven gaps, with its own table and its own axiom. This search is about nine times as long as the first, and it is evaluated in parts: the boxes that are left after 3232 bisections are dealt out to 9696 lists, which the compiled code examines as separate tasks, and a theorem states that the inequality holds if the evaluation in parts returns true. The statement that is proved does not depend on the division. The table computed in Lean agrees with the reference table in all 262,144262{,}144 entries, and the version with counters visits 535,332,163535{,}332{,}163 boxes and accepts 267,666,082267{,}666{,}082, the numbers of the C++ program. Four small boxes are again checked by the kernel itself, among them one around the point where a numerical search found the smallest slack of the inequality, about 1.3⋅10−51.3\cdot 10^{-5}.

Proposition 6.3 is proved by a third run, with its own table and its own axiom. The table computed in Lean agrees with the reference table in all 262,144262{,}144 entries, and the version with counters visits 572,959,453572{,}959{,}453 boxes and accepts 286,479,727286{,}479{,}727, again the numbers of the C++ program. Four small boxes are checked by the kernel itself here too, two of them around the two points where a numerical search found the smallest slack, about 1.0⋅10−51.0\cdot 10^{-5} and 2.0⋅10−52.0\cdot 10^{-5}.

Axioms and size. For each of the six theorems the command #print axioms lists the three standard axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and one axiom of a computation. That axiom records that the evaluation of checkAll kTabArray, or of checkAllPar kTabArray 32 96 for the second run, returned true, for the table in question: Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2 and the second bound of Theorem 1.4 depend on the first run, Theorem 1.3 and the first bound of Theorem 1.4 on the second, and Theorem 1.5 on the third. Everything else is checked by the kernel; in particular the implications from Propositions 3.3, 5.3 and 6.3 to the theorems and the soundness of the search depend on the three standard axioms only. The proof developments contain no sorry; it occurs only in the five statement files Challenge*.lean, where the proofs are left open by design. The development for Theorem 1.1 has about 13,30013{,}300 lines in 7272 files and the one for Theorem 1.3 about 10,00010{,}000 lines in 5757 files; the library they build on has about 102,000102{,}000. Theorem 1.4 adds about 1,9001{,}900 lines in 1212 files: Lemma 6.1, the two counts of Section 6, and the instances. The development for Theorem 1.5 has about 9,1009{,}100 lines in 5454 files. The statements of Section 2 are formalised for the constants of Section 3, not for general parameters.

The ceilings. Propositions 7.2 and 7.3 are formalised in a separate development, of about 3,4003{,}400 lines in 2323 files. Its six theorems depend on the three standard axioms only; no compiled computation enters. The file ChallengeCeilings.lean states them from Mathlib alone, with the two kernels written out and the two energy constants defined by the integrals in (1.1), and SolutionCeilings.lean proves these statements. The hypothesis of Proposition 7.2 is the definition PairCert, with the arguments ss, x1x_{1}, x2x_{2} and bb: there is a constant C3C_{3} such that the displayed inequality holds for all θ\theta-separated labelled configurations and every R≥0R\geq 0 that bounds their spread, with b​Rb\,R in place of b​spread⁡(Y)b\,\spn(Y). The conclusion is stated with C⁡(f)C(f) as defined there. Two identities connect it with the proofs of the theorems, and both are formalised: C⁡(f)=A+BC(f)=A+B with A=∫f2A=\int f^{2} and B=2​∫01u​R​(u)​𝑑uB=2\int_{0}^{1}uR(u)\,du, which is the change of variables u=s−tu=s-t and is proved for every continuous function, and A+BA+B is the value at λ=1\lambda=1 of the energy constant used in the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3. The trial states have rational positions, the values of K2K^{2} are bounded above through Taylor polynomials in rational arithmetic, and the sums over the periods are treated as in the proof of Proposition 7.2. Two further statements connect the definition with the rest of the paper. An inequality of the form of Theorem 2.6, with any constants in place of ours and with exact kernel values, implies the hypothesis for all pairs; this depends on the standard axioms only. And the certificates of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 satisfy the hypothesis with s=6s=6 and with s=7s=7; these are two statements, one for each theorem, and each depends on the axiom of the respective search. The ceilings are formalised for the separation 1720\frac{17}{20}; the statement of Remark 3.4 about other separations is a written argument.

Not formalised are the quantity Q∗​(f)Q^{*}(f) of Section 7.1 and the passage from periodic states to it, the bounds of Proposition 7.1 for the two earlier windows, Table 3, and Section 7.6, of which only Lemma 7.6 is in the Lean library. Their numerical parts are certified by ball arithmetic with FLINT/Arb [21], outside Lean. For the law of Proposition 7.8 the data are exact rational numbers, and a second program with a different interval library repeats the check. The programs that searched for the law are in Python and, for the local optimisation and for the chains of the second stage, in C++; they are in the accompanying files with their tests, and nothing in the proof depends on their correctness. No statement of this paper rests on unvalidated numerical computation: outside Lean, the computations that enter a proof use exact rational arithmetic or interval arithmetic with rigorous error bounds. Floating point without error control was used only to find the certificates, the trial states and the law.

Nature of this work. This paper builds on the first paper in this series [23]. Like that paper, it is primarily an experiment in AI-assisted mathematical research. The arguments, the computations, the Lean formalisation, the figures and much of the text were developed with substantial assistance from AI systems (OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude) under the author’s direction. The certificate of Proposition 3.3, the separation argument and the telescoping corrections were developed with OpenAI Codex. The formalisation, the analysis of Section 7, the window and the certificate of Theorem 1.3, the figures and much of the text were developed with Anthropic Claude, and drafts of the paper were reviewed by the same systems in the role of referees. The author defined and steered the research programme and takes full responsibility for the content.

Appendix A Certificate data

Tables 7, 8 and 9 give the local data of Proposition 3.3, Tables 10 and 11 those of Proposition 5.3, and Tables 12 and 13 those of Proposition 6.3. All integers in the tables are to be divided by 10610^{6}. The weights and the corrections are symmetric in the labels. For each pair of labels the tables give two continuous piecewise linear functions u0u_{0} and u1u_{1} through their values at the knots 78+j8\frac{7}{8}+\frac{j}{8}, 0≤j≤110\leq j\leq 11; they are linear between knots and vanish at 34\frac{3}{4}, at 198\frac{19}{8} and outside [34,198][\frac{3}{4},\frac{19}{8}]. Then (B0,…,B5)=(u0,u1,−u0−u1,−u0−u1,u1,u0)(B_{0},\dots,B_{5})=(u_{0},\,u_{1},\,-u_{0}-u_{1},\,-u_{0}-u_{1},\,u_{1},\,u_{0}), which satisfies (2.2) identically. For the second window, whose frames have eight points, there are three functions and (B0,…,B6)=(u0,u1,u2,−2​(u0+u1+u2),u2,u1,u0)(B_{0},\dots,B_{6})=(u_{0},\,u_{1},\,u_{2},\,-2(u_{0}+u_{1}+u_{2}),\,u_{2},\,u_{1},\,u_{0}).
